summary: Defines ManageSieve, a protocol for securely managing Sieve email filtering scripts on a remote server. Users often cannot log into mail servers, so this lets them keep several scripts and be warned about scripts with syntax errors. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: You cannot walk into the mail room, so this is a phone line that lets you update your mail sorting rules.

subtitle: A line-based protocol for uploading, listing, activating and checking email filter scripts on a server you cannot log into.

tldr.problem: Sieve scripts filter incoming email, but mail stores are often sealed servers that users cannot log into, so users still need a safe way to update their scripts there.
tldr.mechanism: ManageSieve is a line-oriented protocol over TCP, much like IMAP, with commands to authenticate, upload, check, list, rename, delete and activate scripts, and with SASL and STARTTLS for security.
tldr.outcome: A user can keep several scripts, switch which one is active, and be told about scripts with syntax errors before they are stored. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 7817 and RFC 8553.

today: RFC 5804 is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 7817 and RFC 8553. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the base specification of ManageSieve.

sections.title: Why Scripts Need Remote Management
sections.content:
Sieve scripts let users filter incoming email. The RFC notes that message stores are commonly sealed servers, so users cannot log into them, yet they must be able to update their scripts there. ManageSieve is the protocol that does this securely.

A user may keep several scripts on the server, but only one is used to filter incoming messages. That is the active script. A user can have zero or one active script, and the SETACTIVE command is the only way to change it or to turn Sieve processing off. The RFC gives the example of an everyday script and a special vacation script that can be swapped without uploading anything again.

The protocol also tells the user about syntactically flawed scripts, because the server checks every script before storing it.
sections.eli5: You can keep many sets of sorting rules in the mail room, like a normal set and a holiday set. Only one set is in use at a time, and you tell the mail room which one.

sections.title: Lines, Responses and Response Codes
sections.content:
ManageSieve is a line-oriented protocol much like IMAP or ACAP and runs over TCP. Every interaction is a line ending in CRLF. A command is an atom (the command name) followed by zero or more strings and numbers. Strings can be quoted or sent as literals with a known octet count.

Every client query gets an OK, NO or BYE reply. BYE is used when the server wants to close the connection, for example after too many failed authentication attempts. If a server auto-logs out idle clients, the timeout MUST be no less than 30 minutes after successful authentication.

A reply may carry a machine-readable response code in parentheses, followed by human-readable text. Clients MUST NOT parse the text for meaning, and MUST ignore response codes they do not recognise. Codes are a slash-separated hierarchy, so a client that knows QUOTA but not QUOTA/MAXSCRIPTS treats it as QUOTA.

Examples of defined codes include AUTH-TOO-WEAK, ENCRYPT-NEEDED, QUOTA, REFERRAL, TRANSITION-NEEDED, TRYLATER, ACTIVE, NONEXISTENT, ALREADYEXISTS, TAG and WARNINGS.
sections.eli5: The mail room always answers with yes, no or goodbye. It can also add a short secret code that your computer understands, such as "you used too much space".

sections.title: Connecting, Capabilities and Sessions
sections.content:
A ManageSieve server typically listens on TCP port 4190. Before connecting, a client first tries a DNS SRV lookup for service sieve and protocol tcp (for example _sieve._tcp.example.net.). If that fails, it falls back to ordinary address resolution and uses the default port.

After connecting, the server lists its capabilities, one per line. The server MUST return IMPLEMENTATION, SIEVE and VERSION. Others include SASL (the supported authentication mechanisms), STARTTLS, MAXREDIRECTS, NOTIFY, LANGUAGE and OWNER. For servers compliant with this document, VERSION is 1.0. Clients MUST ignore capabilities they do not understand.

A session starts in the non-authenticated state, where only AUTHENTICATE, CAPABILITY, STARTTLS, LOGOUT and NOOP are valid. Clients may pipeline commands, but AUTHENTICATE, STARTTLS and HAVESPACE may appear only as the last command in a group, with a narrow exception for single-round-trip mechanisms such as PLAIN and EXTERNAL.
sections.eli5: When you phone the mail room, it first tells you what it can do. Until you prove who you are, it only answers a few simple questions.

sections.title: The Script Commands
sections.content:
Once authenticated, a client manages scripts with a small set of commands. Script names are UTF-8 strings of at least one character, and servers MUST accept names of up to 128 Unicode characters without truncating longer ones.

  • PUTSCRIPT uploads a script. It replaces an existing script of the same name only if it succeeds, and it does not make the script active unless it replaces the script that already is.
  • CHECKSCRIPT validates a script without storing it, and does not check quotas.
  • HAVESPACE asks whether a script of a given name and size would fit within the user's quota. An OK is not a guarantee.
  • LISTSCRIPTS returns script names, with ACTIVE appended to the active one.
  • GETSCRIPT returns a script's contents.
  • SETACTIVE makes a script active. An empty name disables the active script.
  • RENAMESCRIPT renames a script; renaming the active script keeps it active.
  • DELETESCRIPT deletes a script, but the server MUST refuse to delete the active script (code ACTIVE).
  • NOOP does nothing but reply, and can echo back a tag.
  • LOGOUT ends the session.

On upload, the server MUST check that the script follows the Sieve grammar and that every extension in its require statements is supported. A script that fails is not stored, and the NO message SHOULD give the line number of the first error. An OK can carry a WARNINGS code for a valid script that may not do what the author intended, and clients SHOULD show that text to the user.

For servers without RENAMESCRIPT, the RFC describes a five-step emulation: list, download, upload under the new name, reactivate if needed, then delete the old one.
sections.eli5: You can hand in a new set of rules, ask to see them, pick which set is in use, rename a set, or throw one away. The mail room reads each new set first and points out the line where you made a mistake.

sections.title: Authentication and TLS
sections.content:
AUTHENTICATE names a SASL mechanism, runs the challenge and response exchange (base-64 encoded), and can optionally set up a security layer. The service name is sieve. Re-authentication is not supported: after one success, further AUTHENTICATE commands get a NO. If one mechanism fails, a client may try another.

For interoperability, clients and servers MUST implement the SCRAM-SHA-1 mechanism and PLAIN over TLS. A client willing to use PLAIN MUST first verify the server's identity, and MUST NOT authenticate with PLAIN if it cannot.

STARTTLS begins a TLS negotiation. Afterwards the server MUST re-issue its capabilities (without STARTTLS) and the client MUST discard what it cached. The same re-issue applies when a SASL security layer is negotiated. Re-issuing protects against a man-in-the-middle who altered the capability list beforehand, and lets the client notice a down-negotiation attack.

During TLS the client MUST check the server's hostname or IP address against the certificate. The certificate's subjectAltName is preferred; use of the Common Name is described as existing practice but deprecated.

An optional UNAUTHENTICATE extension, whose support is RECOMMENDED, returns a session to the non-authenticated state.
sections.eli5: Before the mail room changes your rules, you must prove who you are. You also check that you really reached the real mail room and not an impostor, and you talk in a private code so nobody can listen in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without the encryption and integrity services of SASL or TLS (or an external mechanism), ManageSieve transactions are open to passive observers and to man-in-the-middle attacks that alter data. The RFC suggests that clients and servers be configurable to refuse to transfer sensitive information without strong encryption.

Implementations that support mechanisms vulnerable to eavesdropping, such as PLAIN, MUST support at least one configuration where those mechanisms are not advertised or used without an external security layer such as TLS.

Some failure codes can leak information. TRANSITION-NEEDED can reveal that a user name is valid, so servers SHOULD be able to turn it off or make it not depend on the user. A malicious server can also use it to push a client into sending a bare password, so clients SHOULD be able to disable the password transition feature or warn the user.
sections.eli5: If you talk to the mail room on an open line, anyone could listen or change your rules. So use the private code, and be careful about answers that reveal whether a name is real.

sections.title: Sieve URLs and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC defines a sieve URL scheme. A URL can name a server (sieve:// plus an authority) or a script on a server, optionally with an owner. An empty owner, as in sieve://example.com//script, is different from a missing owner and is reserved for global scripts. The server form is what appears in the REFERRAL response code to point the client at another server.

IANA reserved TCP port 4190 for ManageSieve, registered the sieve URI scheme and the sieve service name for GSSAPI/Kerberos/SASL, and created registries for ManageSieve capabilities and response codes. New entries MUST be specified in a Standards Track or IESG-approved Experimental RFC.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives mail rooms a special kind of address, so a rule set can be pointed to by name, and it reserves a phone number (a port) for them.

SCRIPT COMMANDS AND WHAT THEY DO

items.label: Upload
items.desc: Validate and store a script under a name.

items.label: Validate
items.desc: Check a script without storing it.

items.label: Quota check
items.desc: Ask if a script of a given size fits.

items.label: List
items.desc: Names of scripts, with ACTIVE marked.

items.label: Activate
items.desc: Choose the active script; empty name disables.

items.label: Rename
items.desc: Rename; an active script stays active.

items.label: Delete
items.desc: Remove a script, but never the active one.
